My father is unfortunately on his last leg with his fight with cancer. When he passes I will be inheriting his house. He has a USDA home loan with around $10,000 still owed. From what he says, I could live there with no responsibility to the loan, only the property tax. Once I decide to sell, then I am required to pay off the loan. Do I have to pay taxes on the money I would make on the home? If so, would I pay taxes on what I initially make or what is left after paying the loan? What about life insurance, would I be required to pay taxes on that as well?

I don't know anything about a USDA loan and so I have no idea what he is talking about on that specifically. As a result, anything I say may need some revising, but here are a couple general points on inheritance and on taxes. I am only talking about Federal taxes, too. State taxes are different in each state.

Life insurance is generally not taxed. There are a couple exceptions to this, but I doubt you need to worry about them. One way they are taxed is if the estate is large enough to incur estate tax. Insurance proceeds are generally included in the estate for purposes of this determination unless advanced tax planning was done to put the insurance in certain types of trusts or something. To be subject to the estate tax the estate has to be over $5.49 million in 2017. If your Dad's estate is that large, stop reading what I have to say and go see an estates attorney.

The other way life insurance proceeds may be taxed is if it is a form of permanent (rather than term) insurance and the cash value exceed the death benefit. This is another unusual situation. It normally only occurs with wealthy people who use insurance as a way to invest tax free but who either outlived how old they expected to be or had higher than expected returns within the policy.

So let's assume the life insurance is not taxed. Assuming you are the beneficiary, you get the proceeds in full.

Moving to the house.

First things first. When you sell a house you reside in (as opposed to an investment property), you are only taxed to the extent your proceeds exceed your basis by $250,000 ($500,000 for married couples). The basis in a house is generally what you paid for it (there are adjustments, but let's ignore those). If you paid $150k for a hous and sold it later for $300k, you wouldn't be taxed because your gain was less than $250k.

However, in an inheritance situation, you are even better off. Because instead of having the same basis in the house as your father did, you get to step up the basis to the fair market value on the date you inherit. So unless you sell the house for more than $250k worth above its value when your Dad dies, you shouldn't owe taxes on it either.

These are general rules, though. I have no idea how your Dad's loan figures into it or whether he is right you can stop making payments.
